quick: Prophylaxis 250 IU IM; treatment 3000-6000 IU IM
May be used when indicated (benefit outweighs risk)
summary: Tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG) is a sterile preparation of human immune globulin rich in antibodies to tetanus toxin, given intramuscularly for passive immunization. It is used for post-exposure prophylaxis of tetanus in inadequately immunized people with tetanus-prone wounds, and (in higher doses) as part of the treatment of established tetanus. It provides immediate but temporary protection and does not replace active immunization with tetanus toxoid, which should be given concurrently at a separate site. It is generally well tolerated; injection-site reactions and rare hypersensitivity are the main concerns.
indications: Passive immunization (post-exposure prophylaxis) against tetanus following injury in persons whose immunization is incomplete or uncertain
Treatment of clinically established tetanus (as part of overall management)

dosage.d: 250 IU IM; 500 IU if the wound is heavily contaminated, severe, or treatment is delayed >24 hours
dosage.n: Give tetanus toxoid concurrently at a separate site

dosage.d: 250 IU IM (same as adults); higher 500 IU for high-risk wounds
dosage.n: Dose is not weight-based for prophylaxis

dosage.d: Typically 3000-6000 IU IM as a single total dose (regimens vary by product/guideline)
dosage.n: Part of comprehensive tetanus management (wound care, antibiotics, supportive care)

admin: Administer by deep intramuscular injection only - never intravenously
Use the anterolateral thigh or deltoid; divide large volumes between sites
Give concurrently with tetanus toxoid vaccine but at a separate site with a separate syringe (active-passive immunization)
Have epinephrine and resuscitation equipment available for rare anaphylaxis
Allow refrigerated product to reach room temperature and inspect before use
moa: Tetanus immunoglobulin supplies preformed human antibodies (predominantly IgG) against tetanus toxin. These antibodies neutralize circulating, unbound tetanospasmin, providing immediate passive protection. It cannot neutralize toxin already bound to nerve tissue, so it must be given early and combined with wound debridement, antibiotics and active toxoid immunization.

absolute: History of anaphylactic or severe systemic reaction to human immune globulin
Intravenous administration (product is for IM use)
relative: Isolated IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies (risk of hypersensitivity)
Thrombocytopenia or bleeding disorder where IM injection is hazardous
Known reaction to thimerosal or other excipients

preg: Tetanus immunoglobulin may be used during pregnancy when indicated for a tetanus-prone wound; the benefit of preventing maternal/neonatal tetanus outweighs the theoretical risk, and immune globulins are not known to harm the fetus.
lact: Considered compatible with breastfeeding; immunoglobulins are not expected to pose a risk to the breastfed infant.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is required for renal impairment.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required for hepatic impairment.

moderate: Live attenuated virus vaccines (e.g. measles, mumps, rubella, varicella) - passively acquired antibody may impair the immune response; defer such live vaccines for an appropriate interval after immune globulin
minor: Inactivated vaccines and tetanus toxoid are not affected and should be co-administered (separate sites)
interactions.diagnostics: Passively transferred antibodies can transiently produce positive results in some serological tests.

common: Pain, tenderness, swelling or redness at the injection site
rare: Anaphylaxis (especially in IgA-deficient patients with anti-IgA antibodies)
Nephrotic syndrome (rare reports with immune globulins)

monitoring: Observe for immediate hypersensitivity after injection
Confirm and complete active immunization (toxoid series) as indicated
counsel: This injection gives you immediate, short-term protection against tetanus
You also need the tetanus vaccine (toxoid) now and to complete the full course for lasting protection
Mild soreness, swelling or a slight fever at the injection site is common and settles
Tell the staff at once if you feel faint, develop a rash, swelling or difficulty breathing
Delay any live virus vaccines for a few months and inform future vaccinators that you received immunoglobulin
pk: Protective antibody available immediately after IM injection
Peak serum antibody levels reached within a few days
Passive protection lasts several weeks; does not give lasting immunity
Store refrigerated (2-8 C); do not freeze; protect from light
pearls: Always combine with active immunization (tetanus toxoid) given at a separate site for both immediate and lasting protection
Strictly intramuscular - do not give intravenously
Higher doses (3000-6000 IU) are used to treat established tetanus, alongside wound care, antibiotics and supportive measures
Defer live virus vaccines (e.g. MMR, varicella) for several months after administration
Special caution in IgA-deficient patients due to anaphylaxis risk
missed: Tetanus immunoglobulin is generally a single dose given as soon as possible after a tetanus-prone injury; there is no maintenance schedule to miss. If wound prophylaxis was indicated but not given, administer it as soon as the need is recognised, the earlier the better.
overdose: Overdose is unlikely to be harmful given the nature of immune globulin; excess merely provides surplus passive antibody. Manage any local or hypersensitivity reaction supportively.
